316.title: Abu Bakr's collection
316.hook: after many memorizers die in battle, Zayd ibn Thabit gathers it into one copy
316.howItsDone: Muslims teach the collection under Abu Bakr as the moment the Qur'an's written pieces and memorizers were brought together into one set of sheets, and remember Zayd ibn Thabit as the companion who carried it out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scribes: verses on palm stalks and bone, and held by heart. Your line was on bone and heart. Did you say your verse once more before sleep? Day three hundred sixteen.

Think of a family recipe that lives in one grandmother's head. There are notes on the backs of old envelopes, but she's the one who really knows it. Then one winter the family realizes: if we lose her, we lose it. Somebody has to sit down and gather it before it's too late. Now picture that fear across a whole community, about a book they believe is the word of God. Today: Abu Bakr's collection.
screen: `A RECIPE IN ONE HEAD.` → `IF WE LOSE HER, WE LOSE IT.` → `ABU BAKR'S COLLECTION.`

segments.voice: In 632 the Prophet ﷺ died, and Abu Bakr became the first caliph. Within about a year the Muslims fought a hard battle at a place called Yamamah, and many who knew the Qur'an by heart were killed. Zayd ibn Thabit tells what happened next, in a report in Bukhari. Umar came to Abu Bakr, alarmed. If more memorizers fall, he said, much of the Qur'an could be lost; it should be collected. Abu Bakr hesitated. How can we do something the Messenger of God did not do? Umar kept urging, until, Abu Bakr said, God opened his heart to it. Then they sent for Zayd: young, trusted, and one of those who had written the revelation for the Prophet. Zayd's reply is one of the most human lines in the story. By God, if they had asked me to move a mountain, it would not have been heavier. But he did it. He searched it out from the same places we heard yesterday: palm stalks, flat stones and the chests of men. Other reports say he accepted no written piece unless witnesses confirmed it. He tells us he found the closing verses of the ninth surah written with only one man, Abu Khuzaymah al-Ansari. The result was a set of sheets, gathered in one place. They stayed with Abu Bakr until he died, then with Umar, then with Umar's daughter Hafsah, one of the Prophet's widows. And notice what Muslims say this collection was not. It wasn't new words, or an edit. It was the same Qur'an already recited and written, brought from many places into one. Gathered.
screen: `THE BATTLE OF YAMAMAH` · `HOW CAN WE DO WHAT HE DID NOT?` · `HEAVIER THAN A MOUNTAIN` · `SHEETS KEPT BY HAFSAH`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather something scattered. It can be small. The loose papers on a table. The photos of someone you love, spread across three devices. The verses you've learned this year, scattered through your days. Sit, breathe, and bring one scattered thing together in your mind: what are the pieces, and where are they? After the bell, gather them into one place. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the people who kept what mattered. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr's collection. After the battle of Yamamah, Zayd ibn Thabit gathered the Qur'an from its scattered writings and memorizers into one set of sheets. Today's word.
Your line: gathered. Today, find one thing that lives only in someone's memory, a story, a recipe, a name, and ask them to tell you, so it's held in two places. Day three hundred sixteen.

317.title: Uthman's copies
317.hook: the caliph Uthman has standard copies sent to the cities
317.howItsDone: Muslims read from a mushaf whose text follows the copies Uthman sent to the cities, and printed copies usually note that they follow the Uthmani script.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr's collection: Zayd gathering the Qur'an into one set of sheets, kept in the end by Hafsah. Your line was gathered. Did you ask someone for a story only they remember? Day three hundred seventeen.

In the time of the caliph Uthman, a commander named Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman came back from a campaign far to the north, in Armenia and Azerbaijan. What alarmed him there wasn't the fighting. Soldiers from Syria and soldiers from Iraq had been reciting the Qur'an differently from one another, and quarreling about it, each side sure the other was wrong. He went straight to the caliph, Uthman, in Medina. Today: Uthman's copies.
screen: `A COMMANDER COMES HOME WORRIED.` → `TWO ARMIES, TWO WAYS OF RECITING.` → `STRAIGHT TO THE CALIPH.`

segments.voice: Hudhayfah's plea, as Bukhari records it, was this: rescue this community before they differ over the Book the way earlier peoples differed. Uthman acted. He sent to Hafsah for the sheets gathered under Abu Bakr. He set Zayd ibn Thabit to work again, now with three men of Quraysh. His instruction: where you differ with Zayd over how to write a word, write it in the dialect of Quraysh, because the Qur'an came down in their tongue. They made copies, and Uthman sent one to each of the main cities, such as Kufa, Basra and Damascus, and kept one in Medina. Reports differ on how many: four, five, seven. He returned the sheets to Hafsah and ordered other personal copies burned, so there would be one standard. That was hard for some. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud was unhappy at first about giving up his own copy. Yet over time the companions accepted Uthman's text, and Ali is reported to have said he would have done the same. The word for such a copy is mushaf, from sahifah, a sheet. A mushaf is the bound, written Qur'an, the thing on the shelf. Muslims today say the text in every mushaf follows Uthman's copies, and its spelling is called the Uthmani script. And old copies survive. Tradition links some very old copies, kept today in places like Istanbul and Tashkent, to Uthman's time; researchers debate their dates. One text, many cities.
screen: `HUDHAYFAH'S ALARM` · `ZAYD AND THREE MEN OF QURAYSH` · `A COPY FOR EACH CITY` · `MUSHAF: THE WRITTEN COPY`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an old manuscript page. A copy carried by camel to a city far away, set down in a mosque, read aloud to people who never met the Prophet. And the same words reaching you, today. Breathe with that distance. The bell holds the time.
Mushaf. A written, bound copy of the Qur'an, from sahifah, a sheet. Muslims hold that every mushaf today follows the text of Uthman's copies. Today's word.
Your line: one text, many cities. Today, think of people far away reading the same words you know, in cities you may never visit, and let the world feel a little smaller. Day three hundred seventeen.

318.title: Dots and vowels
318.hook: dots and vowel marks were added later to help new readers
318.howItsDone: Muslims today read from copies with full dots and vowel marks, and learners, especially those who didn't grow up with Arabic, rely on those marks to recite correctly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mushaf: Uthman's copies, one standard sent out to the cities. Your line was one text, many cities. Did the world feel a little smaller? Day three hundred eighteen.

Three Arabic letters: ba, ta, tha. In a modern mushaf they have exactly the same shape, a little boat. The only difference is the dots: one below for ba, two above for ta, three above for tha. Now take the dots away. That's close to what the earliest copies looked like: the bones of the words, with the reader supplying the rest from what they'd learned by ear. Today: dots and vowels.
screen: `BA, TA, THA: ONE SHAPE.` → `ONLY THE DOTS DIFFER.` → `NOW TAKE THE DOTS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Early Arabic writing was a kind of shorthand. Many letters shared a shape, and the dots that tell them apart were used sparingly. Short vowels weren't written at all. For the first Muslims that wasn't a problem: the Qur'an lived in their mouths, learned from teachers, and the page was a reminder of what they already knew. But as Islam spread to people whose first language wasn't Arabic, the tradition says, mistakes in recitation began. Tradition credits a scholar of Basra, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, in the first Islamic century, with the first vowel marks: colored dots, often red, placed above, below or beside a letter to show its sound. Later, in the time of the governor al-Hajjaj, scholars are said to have added the dots that tell similar letters apart more fully. And in the next century, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad of Basra, who also mapped the meters of Arabic poetry, gave the vowels the small shapes still used today: a slanting stroke above, a tiny curl like a waw, a stroke below. Sources tell the details differently. But in every telling, the text itself stays put: the marks were added around it, the way you might add pronunciation guides to a poem for a new reader. Some scholars at the time disliked writing anything extra inside the mushaf. In the end the community accepted the marks, because they served the recitation that had been passed down. Each dot was put there for a learner.
screen: `THE SAME SHAPE, DIFFERENT DOTS` · `A PAGE THAT REMINDED, NOT TAUGHT` · `RED DOTS FOR VOWELS` · `MARKS ADDED AROUND THE TEXT`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the dots above the letters. If you have a mushaf or an app, open any page and just look. Don't try to read. Find the dots: one, two, three, above and below. Find the tiny vowel strokes. Notice how much of the page is made of these small marks, placed there for someone learning. If there's no page in front of you, picture ba, ta and tha, three little boats told apart only by their dots. Rest your eyes. The bell holds the time.
Tashkil. Vowel marking — the small strokes added to the Qur'an's script so new readers could recite it rightly. Today's word.
Your line: marks for the reader. Today, add one small mark that helps whoever comes after you: a clear label, a note, a patient word of instruction for someone new. Day three hundred eighteen.

319.title: Arabic, and translation
319.hook: Muslims hold the Qur'an to be the Arabic itself, and a translation to be its meanings
319.howItsDone: Muslims recite the Qur'an in Arabic in prayer everywhere in the world, and read translations, often printed beside the Arabic, as translations of its meanings rather than as the Qur'an itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dots and vowels, tashkil: marks added around the text so new readers could recite it rightly. Your line was marks for the reader. Did you leave one helpful mark for someone? Day three hundred nineteen.

Pick up an English Qur'an in a bookstore and look closely at the title page. On many copies, it doesn't simply say The Qur'an. It says something like The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, or The Meanings of the Qur'an in English. That isn't modesty for its own sake. It's a careful statement of what Muslims believe the book in your hands is, and what it isn't. Today: Arabic, and translation.
screen: `LOOK AT THE TITLE PAGE.` → `THE MEANING OF…` → `WHAT THE BOOK IS, AND ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Muslims hold that the Qur'an is the word of God in Arabic: not only its ideas, but its actual words, sounds and order. The Qur'an says so about itself. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We have revealed it, a Lecture in Arabic, that ye may understand." Lecture is Pickthall's old word for a reading, a recitation; the Arabic there is qur'an. So a translation, however good, is a human attempt to carry the meanings into another language. It's valuable, often essential, but Muslims don't call it the Qur'an itself. That's why Marmaduke Pickthall, whose English you've heard all year, called his 1930 work The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, and wrote in his foreword, in effect, that the Qur'an cannot be translated and his book was only an attempt to present its meaning. This shapes practice. The ritual prayer is said in Arabic wherever a Muslim lives, which is why children in Jakarta and Chicago learn al-Fatiha in the same sounds. The schools of law hold that a translation can't stand in for the Arabic in the prayer's recitation, though a few early jurists made allowance for someone who couldn't yet manage it; du'a, personal prayer, can be in any language. And it shapes how Muslims read. Arabic words often hold several layers at once. Commentators explain rabb, in the Fatiha, as lord, and also the one who raises and nurtures. English has to choose, and every choice leaves something behind. So readers often keep a translation open beside the Arabic, and learn a little Arabic even without becoming fluent, to hear what the translation is pointing at. A translation is a meaning: a way toward the words, not the words themselves.
screen: `THE MEANING OF THE GLORIOUS KORAN` · `A LECTURE IN ARABIC` · `THE PRAYER IS SAID IN ARABIC` · `EVERY TRANSLATION CHOOSES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a verse in two translations. After the bell, look up one short verse, al-Ikhlas is a good one, in two English translations, and notice where they choose different words. For now, sit with one Arabic word you know: bismillah, or alhamdulillah. Say it softly. Then say one English meaning of it. Then another. Notice whether either English fills the Arabic. Let the Arabic sit on its own for the last few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Arabic. The language Muslims hold the Qur'an was revealed in: the words themselves, not only their meaning. Today's word.

Your line: a translation is a meaning. Today, when you read or hear something translated, a verse, a song, a friend's message, ask what the original might hold that the translation had to leave behind. Day three hundred nineteen.

320.title: Pickthall and the 1934 translation
320.hook: two early English translations, both by Muslims, both still read
320.howItsDone: Many English-speaking Muslims read the Qur'an's meanings in more than one translation, often Pickthall's 1930 rendering alongside the 1934 translation and newer ones, usually printed beside the Arabic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arabic: the Qur'an as the Arabic itself, and a translation as its meanings. Your line was a translation is a meaning. What did a translation leave behind for you? Day three hundred twenty.

All year, when this path has quoted the Qur'an in English, you've heard one particular voice. Thee and thou. Lo! Verily. "But lo! with hardship goeth ease." That's Marmaduke Pickthall, an Englishman whose translation was published in 1930. Why him? Partly because his translation is old enough to be free for anyone to quote. But it's also one of two early English translations, both by Muslims, that people still read nearly a century later. Today: Pickthall, and the translation of 1934.
screen: `THEE, THOU, LO, VERILY.` → `AN ENGLISHMAN, PUBLISHED 1930.` → `TWO EARLY TRANSLATIONS.`

segments.voice: Pickthall was the son of an English country clergyman. He became a novelist, traveled in Syria, Palestine and Turkey, and grew to love the Muslim world he met there. In London, during the First World War, he publicly declared himself a Muslim. Later he went to India and worked in the service of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who gave him leave to finish his translation. Before publishing, he took it to Cairo to go over it with scholars there. It appeared in 1930 as The Meaning of the Glorious Koran. His aim was to be almost literal, close to the Arabic's order, in the solemn English of the old Bible that his readers would recognize as scripture. That's why it can feel stiff, and why it can also feel like thunder. The second came from an Indian Muslim scholar who had served in the civil service in India, and began appearing in 1934. Its English is more flowing, with a rhythm close to poetry, and it carries long explanatory notes, so reading it is like reading with a teacher at your shoulder. Later publishers revised some of those notes, so editions differ, and readers check which one they hold. Two Muslims, two temperaments. One stays close to the Arabic's shape and lets you do the work. One opens the meaning out and explains as it goes. And that's the gift of reading more than one. Where they agree, you're probably close to the meaning. Where they differ, you've found a place where the Arabic holds more than one English sentence can carry.
screen: `AN ENGLISH NOVELIST BECOMES MUSLIM` · `ALMOST LITERAL, IN OLD ENGLISH` · `A SECOND VOICE, FROM 1934` · `WHERE THEY DIFFER, LOOK CLOSER`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line in each. Start with Pickthall's line from Surah 94: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease." Say it slowly, twice, and listen to the old English: goeth, not goes. After the bell, find the same verse in the 1934 translation, or any other you have, and read the two side by side. For now, stay with this one line. Notice the word with: not after hardship, but with it. If something is hard for you right now, set it beside that word, and let the line sit there. The bell holds the time.
Pickthall and the 1934 translation. Two early English renderings of the Qur'an's meanings, both by Muslims: one close and plain, one flowing and explained. Today's word.

Your line: two voices, one line. Today, when two people you trust describe the same thing differently, listen to both, and look for what each one sees that the other doesn't. Day three hundred twenty.

321.title: Explaining it
321.hook: scholars explain verses by other verses, hadith, language and context
321.howItsDone: Muslims read tafsir, commentary on the Qur'an, in study circles, in Friday sermons and at home; classic commentaries like those of al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir are widely read and translated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pickthall and the translation of 1934: two Muslims, two temperaments. Your line was two voices one line. Did you hear out someone who saw it differently? Day three hundred twenty-one.

A verse says that those who believe, and don't mix their belief with wrongdoing, are the ones who will be safe. When the companions heard it, they were frightened. Which of us, they asked, has never done wrong? If that's the condition, who is safe? They took the question straight to the Prophet ﷺ. His answer didn't come out of nowhere. He pointed them to another verse. Today: explaining it.
screen: `WHICH OF US HAS NEVER DONE WRONG?` → `THEY TOOK IT TO THE PROPHET.` → `HE POINTED TO ANOTHER VERSE.`

segments.voice: The Prophet told them: it isn't what you think. Haven't you heard what Luqman said to his son? And he recited from Surah 31, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong." The wrong meant in the first verse was that one: setting up partners with God, not every everyday failing. The companions could breathe again. That story, in Bukhari, is the seed of tafsir, explaining the Qur'an. The word comes from a root meaning to uncover, to lay open. And scholars have climbed the same ladder ever since. First, the Qur'an explains the Qur'an: one verse opens another, as Luqman's line opened the first. Second, the Prophet's words and example, the hadith. Third, the understanding of the companions who were there, like Ibn Abbas, for whom the Prophet prayed that he be given understanding of the religion. Fourth, the Arabic language itself: grammar, rare words, even old Arabic poetry, which Ibn Abbas is reported to have used to explain unusual words. And context: the occasions of revelation you met eleven days ago. From these came the great written commentaries. Al-Tabari, in the tenth century, gathered the early reports verse by verse into a huge work. Ibn Kathir, in the fourteenth, wrote one of the most read commentaries, and it still is. Others focus on law, or language, or the inner meanings the Sufis looked for. And scholars warn against explaining the Qur'an by personal opinion alone, without knowledge. Tafsir isn't a way of adding to the book. It's a way of listening to it more closely, letting its own verses, and the people nearest to it, speak first.
screen: `LUQMAN'S LINE OPENS THE VERSE` · `THE QUR'AN EXPLAINS THE QUR'AN` · `HADITH, COMPANIONS, LANGUAGE` · `AL-TABARI AND IBN KATHIR`

Let another verse come to mind, or just let the question sit. The bell holds the time.
Tafsir. Explaining the Qur'an, from a root meaning to uncover: by the Qur'an itself, the hadith, the companions and the language. Today's word.

Your line: the book explains itself. Today, when something someone says puzzles you, before deciding what they meant, look at what else they've said. Let them explain themselves. Day three hundred twenty-one.

322.title: The styles of recitation
322.hook: several authentic readings, passed down in chains of reciters
322.howItsDone: Many printed copies follow the reading of Hafs from Asim, copies in parts of North and West Africa follow Warsh from Nafi', and specialist reciters learn several readings from teachers with a chain of transmission back to the Prophet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tafsir: explaining the Qur'an, its own verses speaking first. Your line was the book explains itself. Did you let someone explain themselves? Day three hundred twenty-two, the end of a week.

In the Prophet's lifetime, Umar ibn al-Khattab heard a man named Hisham reciting Surah al-Furqan in the prayer, and some of the words came out differently from the way Umar had learned them from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself. Umar was so upset he could barely wait for the prayer to end. When it did, he took Hisham by his cloak and marched him straight to the Prophet. Today: the styles of recitation.

segments.voice: The Prophet asked Hisham to recite. Then he said: this is how it was revealed. He asked Umar to recite. And he said again: this is how it was revealed. Then he explained that the Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf, seven modes, so recite whichever is easy for you. The story is in Bukhari. Scholars have discussed for centuries exactly what the seven ahruf were, and there's no single agreed answer. But within those permitted ways stand what are called the qira'at, the readings. Each is a way of reciting the same Qur'an, traced from teacher to student in a chain back to the Prophet. The differences are small: a vowel, a letter, how long a sound is held. In al-Fatiha, for instance, some readers recite maliki yawm al-din, King of the Day, and others maaliki, Owner of the Day. Both are accepted, and the tradition hears both as true of God. In the tenth century, a scholar in Baghdad, Ibn Mujahid, set out seven famous readers; later scholars recognized ten. Each has two main transmitters, whose names identify the reading. Many printed copies today follow the reading of Hafs from Asim; in parts of North and West Africa, copies and reciters follow Warsh from Nafi'. In the tradition these aren't rival versions. They're held to be the Qur'an itself, recited in the ways the Prophet taught. Many voices, one text. Now look back at the week. Abu Bakr's collection gathered it. Uthman's copies spread it. Dots and vowels helped new readers. Arabic, and translation. Pickthall and the 1934 translation. Tafsir, explaining it. And now the readings: the living voice under the page.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to two reciters. After the bell, find al-Fatiha recited by two different people, perhaps one in the reading of Hafs and one in Warsh, and listen for what changes and what doesn't. For now, if you've heard someone recite, remember that voice: in a mosque, a video, a relative's kitchen. If you haven't, remember any voice you love hearing read aloud. Hear it in your mind. Then picture another voice, somewhere else in the world, reciting the same surah at this same moment. The bell holds the time.
Qira'at. The readings: accepted ways of reciting the same Qur'an, each passed down in a chain of teachers back to the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: many voices, one text. Today, when you hear something familiar said in an unfamiliar accent or way, listen for what's the same underneath. Day three hundred twenty-two.
